subtitle: "Could any of it replace or complement BibVik's existing methods?"

> **Note:** This document was drafted with the assistance of Claude (Anthropic,
> claude-sonnet-5, August 2026) and reviewed by the project author. All cited
> sources were independently verified to exist before inclusion. No sources
> have been inferred or hallucinated.

## Summary (read this first)

Christian Boulanger (Max Planck Institute for Legal History and Legal Theory,
mpilhlt) and collaborators, chiefly Luca Foppiano (ScienciaLAB), build reference-
extraction tooling for law and humanities scholarship — the same structural
problem BibVik has (footnote-embedded citations, poor bibliometric database
coverage, non-English material). Their public work was reviewed piece by piece
against BibVik's pipeline to see what, if anything, is worth adopting.

**Verdict: adopt narrowly, mostly for what it teaches rather than what it
runs.**

- **Worth doing:** use `llamore`'s F1 evaluation harness (fuzzy string +
  Hungarian matching) to finally get a measured accuracy number for BibVik's
  own detection/postprocess methods, none of which currently have one.
- **Worth trying, bounded:** run `tei-bibl-annotator` (a small fine-tuned
  model that tags author/title/date spans in a raw citation string) against
  the backlog of ~167 `llm_from_footnote` entries with blank title and blank
  `_raw_citation`, after splitting the compound citations those footnotes
  contain. Low cost, low risk, narrow scope — and the hard diagnostic work on
  that backlog is already done by hand (see Decision_log, 2026-08-11 entry).
- **Not worth adopting:** the retrained GROBID footnote-segmentation model
  (targets a weakness BibVik's Method 5 already routes around by not
  depending on GROBID zoning at all), the TOC-extraction model (German-only
  training data, a dead end for our multilingual corpus), and `pdf-tei-editor`
  as an annotation workbench (plugin architecture still mid-refactor; would
  mean restructuring our correction workflow for uncertain gain).
- **Not touched at all:** detection itself — deciding whether a span of text
  *is* a citation, in six languages, embedded in archaeological prose. None
  of Boulanger's tools do this; it's a different problem from the one his
  tools solve (structuring a citation string you've already isolated).
- **The stated bottleneck (his own words):** *"It's all experimental though,
  nothing is production-ready. As I said, annotated footnote data is the key
  to progress, and it's the hardest to come by."* We have exactly the kind
  of annotated data he lacks — multilingual, non-legal, non-German — as a
  byproduct of our own correction workflow. A joint annotation effort is a
  more realistic path forward than adopting his checkpoints as-is.

The rest of this document is the full reasoning behind each of those calls.

---

## Why this was worth looking into

Christian Boulanger posted about a fine-tuned vision-language model for
extracting table-of-contents structure from scanned book pages
([sciences.social/@cmboulanger/117149370355856933](https://sciences.social/@cmboulanger/117149370355856933)),
which is directly relevant to BibVik's `CitationAnalysis` pipeline: book
chapters have historically poor metadata coverage, and BibVik already has to
manually decide whether to treat a book as one bloated entry or decompose it
into its constituent chapters (see `research-protocol.qmd`'s discussion of
this). His broader body of work — spread across
[github.com/cboulanger](https://github.com/cboulanger),
[github.com/mpilhlt](https://github.com/mpilhlt), and
[huggingface.co/cmboulanger](https://huggingface.co/cmboulanger) — targets
the same structural gap BibVik exists to work around: standard bibliometric
databases (Scopus, WoS, OpenAlex, CrossRef) have poor coverage of footnote-
heavy, non-English, humanities/monograph literature.

## Who's involved and how real this is

Boulanger runs the "Legal Theory Knowledge Graph" project at mpilhlt since
2022, aimed at producing machine-readable data on socio-legal theory
scholarship. His main collaborator is Luca Foppiano (ScienciaLAB, Portugal;
GROBID/document-ML background), with Andreas Wagner (mpilhlt), Anselm Küsters
(University of Stuttgart), and others in supporting roles. The work is real
and active, not vaporware: `pdf-tei-editor` has 1,300+ commits and 78
releases; the FOSSIL dataset/paper (Foppiano & Boulanger, arXiv 2606.01109,
May 2026) reports actual measured results; the HuggingFace models come with
quantified, honestly-reported evaluation numbers rather than marketing
claims. But it is explicitly experimental — Boulanger's own assessment, from
a public post: *"It's all experimental though, nothing is production-ready.
As I said, annotated footnote data is the key to progress, and it's the
hardest to come by."* The evaluation numbers that exist are small-sample
(FOSSIL's end-to-end eval is 4 documents) and single-domain (German legal-
sociology footnotes, or German-only book TOCs) — nothing has been tested on
archaeology or on Scandinavian-language material.

## Piece-by-piece assessment

### GROBID footnote flavour / FOSSIL specialization

A retrained version of GROBID's article-*segmentation* model (the stage that
decides whether a zone of a page is `<body>`, `<footnote>`, `<listBibl>`,
etc.), trained on FOSSIL, a 96-document, multi-language (English, Portuguese,
Italian, German), multi-discipline SSH corpus with real footnote-embedded
citations. Checked directly against the actual training PDFs
(`grobid-footnote-flavour/batches/`): DOIs resolve to journals like *German
History* (Oxford), *Medical Law Review*, *Sociological Review*, *Historical
Social Research*, and Italian-language humanities journals — genuinely
multi-disciplinary within SSH, but no archaeology and no Scandinavian-language
material.

**What it actually fixes:** stock GROBID, trained mostly on STEM papers where
footnotes are rare short asides, often mislabels a footnote-heavy page's
footnote zone as ordinary body text — so that content never reaches GROBID's
citation parser at all, correct or not. The retrained model is better at
correctly zoning footnote content so it gets a chance to be parsed. This is a
segmentation/plumbing fix, not a citation-recognition or parsing improvement
— FOSSIL's own reported gains are almost entirely in *recall* (content that
was previously invisible is now seen), not precision (what happens once it's
seen — splitting bundled citations, filtering non-citation commentary — 
remains a stated open problem, along with cross-reference resolution
generally, e.g. "Ibid.", "see n. 9").

**Why this doesn't matter much for BibVik specifically:** Method 5 (LLM
Footnote Extraction) already reaches footnote content independent of GROBID's
zoning, by sending footnotes to an LLM directly rather than depending on
GROBID's segmentation to route them correctly first. BibVik built around
this exact weakness without knowing this fix existed. The flavour's benefit
would only show up in improving what reaches Methods 1/2 (GROBID
bibliography, GROBID inline markers) — a real but narrow effect, testable
cheaply against the 20 F1 papers already known to have empty reference divs
(`architecture.qmd`, Method 6 weaknesses), but not worth prioritizing.

**A closer look at the actual annotated footnote data** (viewed directly,
not just described secondhand from the paper) showed something more useful
than the segmentation fix itself: real footnote-embedded citations are not
just "differently formatted" versions of bibliography entries. They're
embedded in continuous prose, broken across page boundaries, share a text
block with unrelated content (author biographical blurbs, quotations,
running-header page numbers physically interleaved with citation text), and
frequently bundle more than one work into what reads as a single footnote
(e.g. "AUD 1996, 242; AUD 1997, 153–154; Graham-Campbell 2004, 362; Baastrup
2010b" — four separate works run together with no clean delimiter beyond
punctuation). This is a more concrete and more useful picture of the failure
mode than "footnote-style references," and is worth keeping as a reference
point when characterizing BibVik's own footnote data — independent of
whether the flavour itself is ever adopted.

**Verdict: not worth pursuing as a priority.** Test only against the 20
empty-reference-div papers if curious; don't commit pipeline changes around
it.

### `tei-bibl-annotator`

A LoRA fine-tune of Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct that takes one raw citation string
and wraps XML tags around the author/title/date spans within it. It does not
find citations, does not decide what counts as a citation, and does not
split compound/bundled citation strings — it only tags structure in a string
already handed to it, one string at a time. Measured on a 1,207-record
held-out set: 99.83% well-formed XML output, 42.5% exact match against gold
markup. Trained on German (mostly) legal-sociology footnote citations, plus
some English — untested on archaeology or Scandinavian languages, and the
domain gap is real (its whole training set is legal citation conventions,
not ours).

**Direct comparison against BibVik's own code:** `postprocess.py`'s
`recover_authors_from_raw()` and `recover_titles_from_raw()` do the same
task — extract structured fields from a raw citation string — via a bare
prompt to a general chat model (`qwen2.5:7b`), with no confidence score
beyond a binary success/fail flag and no gold set anywhere in the pipeline
to check accuracy against. This is the same failure pattern already
documented elsewhere in BibVik: `docs/methods/resolver.md` records that an
earlier CrossRef-based resolution approach was scrapped after an audit found
70–80% false positives — i.e., unvalidated automated resolution has already
burned this project once. `tei-bibl-annotator`'s 42.5% is not necessarily
better than what the current prompt achieves on BibVik's material — the
honest point is that it's *measured* and BibVik's current approach isn't.

**Concrete opening:** the ~167-entry `llm_from_footnote` cluster (title and
`_raw_citation` both blank) is exactly the shape of input this model expects,
once split. Root cause (see Decision_log, 2026-08-11) is that a footnote
citing several works in one string produces one blank entry per citekey
instead of being split into its components; the raw footnote text survives
in `_source_footnote` even when parsing failed, so this is a structuring
problem, not a data-loss problem. Plan: (1) rule-based split on the
semicolon/clause pattern these compound footnotes use — cheap, not an LLM
call; (2) run `tei-bibl-annotator` on each resulting fragment; (3) feed
results into `corrections.yaml` as `_draft: true` candidates for the normal
review workflow, never auto-applied.

**Important scoping note:** by the time this was investigated, the
diagnostic work on this backlog was already substantially done by hand —
24 of the original 98-entry sub-batch were closed out through
`raw_citation` cross-checks and `cited_by` provenance review, and the
underlying compound-footnote mechanism was already identified. What
`tei-bibl-annotator` could still help with is the comparatively mechanical
remainder (structuring the split fragments), not the harder diagnostic work,
which is finished.

**Verdict: worth a bounded experiment**, evaluated against a gold subset
using `llamore`'s F1 class before trusting its output for anything more than
draft corrections.

### `nuextract3-toc`

A LoRA fine-tune of NuExtract3 (Qwen3.5-based vision-language model) that
extracts `{title, authors, page_number}` entries from a table-of-contents
page image. Measured on a 44-book held-out split: F1 0.7544 (up from a 0.6783
zero-shot baseline), with the gain almost entirely in precision (the base
model over-generates entries). **Trained exclusively on German-language book
TOCs**; the model card itself warns of degraded quality outside that domain.

This directly addresses a real BibVik problem — deciding whether an edited
volume should be treated as one bloated F1/F2 node or decomposed into
per-chapter entries, flagged as a concern in `research-protocol.qmd`'s
discussion of vetting books for Grobid processing. A TOC extractor could
correctly decompose a volume's structure before citations are attributed to
it. But it does not solve the harder adjacent problem — reattaching a
unified, volume-level bibliography's entries back to the specific chapter
that actually cited each one — which remains unsolved by anything in
Boulanger's toolkit or elsewhere.

**Verdict: dead end for BibVik as-is.** The German-only training data rules
it out for a corpus that is Norwegian/Swedish/Danish/German/French/English,
and fine-tuning a replacement for our own languages is not a small
undertaking. Not worth pursuing unless a future joint project with
Boulanger made producing multilingual TOC training data a shared goal in its
own right (see "The data problem" below).

### `pdf-tei-editor`

A full web-based PDF/TEI annotation tool (dual-pane viewer, versioning,
role-based access, plugin architecture for pluggable extraction backends
including GROBID and `llamore`). Active and substantial (1,300+ commits, 78
releases, most recent within the last month), but its own developer
documentation (`docs/history/plugin-architecture-simplification.md`)
describes the frontend plugin system as still absorbing two coexisting
architectural patterns, with backward compatibility as an explicit, ongoing
commitment rather than a settled state. Backend (Python/FastAPI) plugins
look more stable than frontend (JavaScript) plugins.

**Verdict: not worth adopting as BibVik's annotation environment.** Would
mean restructuring the existing `corrections.yaml` workflow around someone
else's UI and access-control model, for a plugin API that is still visibly
in flux. If BibVik ever needs a proper human-correction UI (beyond
hand-editing YAML), worth a second look once the frontend plugin
architecture has settled — check for backward-compatibility violations
before adopting even then.

### `llamore`

A Python package (importable via `pip install llamore`) with two useful,
independent parts: (1) reference extractors pluggable to various LLM/VLM
backends, and (2) an `F1` evaluation class using Levenshtein-based fuzzy
matching and Hungarian (optimal bipartite) matching to score extracted
references against gold labels — confirmed by reading
`src/llamore/metrics.py` directly, it has no hard dependency on GROBID or
`pdf-tei-editor` and can be pointed at any `Reference` objects, including
BibVik's own output.

**Verdict: the single highest-value adoption**, and the one with zero domain
risk. BibVik currently has no measured accuracy for any of its six detection
methods or its LLM-based postprocess passes — everything is validated by
spot-checking, not by a number. Hand-annotating even ~50 entries from the
existing corpus and scoring current methods (and, if tried,
`tei-bibl-annotator`) against that gold set with `llamore`'s `F1` class would
answer, for the first time, whether any given method is actually working as
well as assumed.

### FOSSIL (the dataset itself, distinct from the model trained on it)

96 annotated scholarly articles, ~7,600 footnote-embedded references,
CC0-licensed, English/Portuguese/Italian/German, 1959–2025. Not directly
usable — contains no archaeology and no Scandinavian-language material, so
none of it can be merged into BibVik's bibliography or used as gold data for
our corpus. Its value here is entirely as a **template**: a documented,
measured, five-phase annotation workflow (pre-annotate with GROBID → correct
→ verify by a senior reviewer → integrate feedback into a living guide,
tracked via GitHub issues → retrain), with real inter-annotator-agreement
statistics (Krippendorff's α = 0.917 across 194 comparisons, 96 documents, 7
annotators) run before the resulting data was trusted for anything. If BibVik
or a joint project ever built its own gold-standard footnote corpus, this is
the concrete precedent to follow, not a document to merely admire.

## The data problem, and whether there's a way around it

Boulanger names the actual bottleneck himself: annotated footnote data,
which is scarce because producing it requires slow, disagreement-prone,
domain-expert annotation work (FOSSIL needed 7 annotators and formal
agreement checks even within one relatively well-defined domain). This is
not a modeling problem his tools can shortcut around; it is a supply
problem.

Three ways to make progress on it, independent of whether Boulanger's
specific checkpoints are ever adopted:

1. **Piggyback on work already happening.** BibVik's `corrections.yaml`
   review process already produces exactly the raw-string-in,
   corrected-structured-fields-out pairs that constitute training data, as a
   byproduct of routine curation. Capturing these systematically (rather
   than only applying the correction and discarding the "before" state)
   would build a gold set at close to zero marginal annotation cost.

2. **Weak supervision from method agreement.** Since BibVik already runs six
   independent detection methods, citations where multiple methods agree
   are a plausible silver-label source requiring no manual annotation;
   effort then concentrates on disagreements. This is broadly the same
   principle behind FOSSIL's own pre-annotate-then-correct workflow, applied
   using BibVik's existing method redundancy instead of a single baseline
   model.

3. **A joint annotation effort, proposed on mutually rational terms.** If a
   small batch of BibVik's non-English monograph/chapter material were
   annotated using `pdf-tei-editor` and a schema compatible with (or
   extending) FOSSIL's, it would produce exactly the multilingual,
   cross-disciplinary annotated data Boulanger says is scarce, while
   yielding a validated extraction approach tuned to our own corpus as the
   direct output. This is a fair trade, not a favour: BibVik has the kind of
   underrepresented material (Scandinavian-language archaeological grey
   literature) that is structurally absent from every dataset cited in the
   FOSSIL paper's own related-work section.

None of these are fast. All three require real annotation hours from
someone. But they are the actual way around the stated bottleneck — not a
better model, more data.

## Open questions for Boulanger, if contact is made

- Does the footnote-flavour GROBID or FOSSIL's specialized segmentation
  generalize at all beyond SSH/law/German-language material — has it been
  tried on archaeology or non-German-language monographs?
- Would he be interested in a small multilingual archaeology TOC/footnote
  annotation collaboration, given the corpus gap on his side?
- What's the actual state of cross-reference resolution ("Ibid.", "see n.
  9") — confirmed from the FOSSIL paper as "largely open" rather than
  merely modest — is there any interim heuristic he'd recommend before it's
  properly solved?
- Is `pdf-tei-editor`'s plugin architecture stable enough to build a
  lightweight custom backend against yet, given the ongoing frontend
  refactor documented in the repo's own history?

## Bottom line

This toolset does not fare well against the bulk of BibVik's current
citation-verification work (the ~900-record manual review), because that
work is fundamentally source-fidelity checking against real PDFs — reading
a document and judging what's actually printed there, reconciling against
existing corpus data, catching fabrications and misattributions. None of
Boulanger's tools do this; they only restructure a string already believed
to be a real citation. Where his tools do bear on BibVik's actual work (the
167-entry blank-title backlog), the expensive diagnostic work is already
done by hand, leaving a narrower, more mechanical opening than it first
appeared. The clearest, lowest-risk, highest-value takeaway is not a tool at
all: adopt `llamore`'s evaluation methodology to put a real number on
methods BibVik has been running on faith.
